channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: S&P Global's flash US manufacturing PMI rose to 57 in September from 53.9 in August, its highest in 52 months, while the composite index reached 58.4, its highest in 62 months.
item.description:
The services PMI rose to 58.7, a 59-month high. MarketScreener reports that the survey's measure of prices paid for inputs rose to a nearly four-year high, and the euro area's flash composite PMI also beat expectations, rising to 53.1 from 52.0. Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said further rate increases are likely needed to bring inflation back to target in a timely fashion, pointing to tariffs, the Middle East conflict, Russia's war on Ukraine and investment demand for AI as sources of price pressure; MarketScreener's account indicates he sees at least two more increases, without saying when. The dollar rose to its highest level since late July on bets of further increases. The reporting does not break the PMI down by industry or say which inputs drove the price measure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

On a general reading, strong activity and rising input prices together are the combination that leads central banks to keep raising rates, and Barr's remarks link a strong economy to rising inflation risks. For an industrial company, the input-price reading is the part that reaches costs first, while higher rates reach customers' investment in construction and equipment with a delay. A stronger dollar also changes the translation of dollar-priced raw materials for European buyers. The PMI is a survey measure of direction and breadth, not a level of output. Points that may be worth considering include how purchasing plans account for input-price pressure reported across US manufacturing, and whether customer investment assumptions allow for the further US rate rises Barr expects.

MarketScreener | Dünya | Commercial Times | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | MarketScreener

item.title: Turkey's Ministry of Trade has imposed final anti-dumping duties on junction boxes for solar panels imported from China, at 38.23% of the CIF price for five named producers and 57.11% for all other Chinese producers, effective 23 September.
item.description:
The five producers named are Zhejiang Twinsel Electronic Technology, Risen Ningbo New Material, QC Solar Suzhou, QC Solar Jiangsu and Zhejiang Chint Xinhui PV. The measure completes a dumping investigation and covers the junction boxes that provide a panel's electrical connection, not complete solar panels. Dünya describes Turkey's solar market as growing rapidly. The reporting does not give import volumes, the share of the Turkish market held by Chinese junction boxes, the duration of the measure, or whether domestic producers can supply the demand.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A duty on one component rather than the whole panel can shift where the panel's parts are sourced and possibly where final assembly takes place, on a general reading. Junction boxes are bonded and potted onto the back of the panel, so a change in their origin can mean changes in the materials used to fix and seal them, which is a general reading rather than something the report states. The measure applies trade defence to a component rather than to the finished panel. Points that may be worth considering include whether solar module customers in Turkey are changing component suppliers, and whether similar component-level measures appear in other markets.

Dünya

item.title: India has reduced basic customs duty on crude soybean and palm oil from 10% to 5%, on refined soybean and palm oil from 32.5% to 27.5%, and removed the 10% duty on crude sunflower oil, effective 24 September.
item.description:
The duty on refined sunflower oil falls to 22.5% from 32.5%. The stated aim is to reduce import costs and potentially ease domestic edible oil prices. The reporting does not give the expected effect on prices, the volume of imports affected, or whether the cuts are temporary. It does not say how exporting countries, mainly for palm oil, are expected to respond, or whether the measure affects non-food uses of these oils.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

India is one of the largest importers of vegetable oils, which is background rather than something the reports state, so a lower duty can raise Indian import demand for palm and soybean oil and affect prices on world markets. Vegetable oils and their derivatives are feedstocks for oleochemicals used in some bio-based raw materials, on a general reading, so the measure bears on bio-based input costs indirectly rather than directly. The duty change is a decision with an effective date; its price effect is not measured in the reporting. Points that may be worth considering include which bio-based raw materials are linked to palm or soybean oil prices, and whether a change in Indian import demand appears in those prices.

The Hindu Business Line | The Economic Times

item.title: The board of Taiwan Cement Corporation has approved the acquisition of IFCEM, the second-largest cement and building materials business in Ukraine, for EUR 750 million.
item.description:
IFCEM sells to neighbouring Eastern European countries, with Poland and Romania its main export markets, and also supplies Moldova, Slovakia and Hungary. Commercial Times reports the purchase as part of chairman Nelson Chang's aim to lead post-war reconstruction in Europe with low-carbon technology. The reporting does not give IFCEM's capacity, revenue or number of plants, the expected closing date, whether regulatory approvals are required, or how the deal is financed. It also does not say whether the plants are currently operating at normal levels during the war.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

An Asian building-materials group paying EUR 750 million for a Ukrainian cement business is an investment decision on the size of Ukrainian and Central European reconstruction demand, taken while the war continues. Cement is not an adhesive, but reconstruction demand extends to construction chemicals — tile adhesives, sealants, waterproofing and insulation systems — which is a general reading rather than something the report states. The export network into Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Hungary makes this a regional supply position as well as a Ukrainian one. Points that may be worth considering include how construction-chemicals supply for Ukraine and neighbouring markets is positioned for reconstruction, and whether building-materials groups entering the region bring their own supplier networks.

Commercial Times

item.title: Honda Motor plans to build a new hybrid vehicle production plant in Ohio, with an expected investment of about JPY 300 billion to 400 billion and production expected to start in 2030.
item.description:
The reporting gives only these points. It does not state the plant's capacity, the models to be built, the number of jobs, whether the site is new or an extension of Honda's existing Ohio operations, or whether the plan has been formally approved by the board. The investment is given as a range, and the reporting does not say what drives the choice of hybrid over pure electric vehicles for the plant. Production is not expected to start before 2030.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A new vehicle assembly plant in the US is a new consumption point for automotive bonding, sealing and coating materials, and the specification choices for a new line are usually made years before production starts, which is a general reading rather than something the report states. The choice of hybrids sits alongside other reporting today in which hybrid and battery-electric demand in Europe rose 27% in August, but the reporting does not give Honda's reasoning. With production in 2030, the plan is a long-term signal about where assembly volume is being added, not a near-term demand change. Points that may be worth considering include when supplier nominations for a plant of this kind are typically made, and how North American automotive plans account for hybrid rather than pure electric growth.

Commercial Times

item.title: Taiwan's Eternal Materials, Topco and Sanfu Chemical are accelerating production expansion for electronic and semiconductor demand, with Eternal's advanced packaging materials business up 109% month on month in August.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that Eternal Materials has two to three products entering mass production and plans a new line in Zhuhai, China, next year for organic silicon microsphere materials used in high-end copper clad laminates above M8, with the goal of doubling capacity from 3,000 to 6,000 tonnes and expanding it to 12,000 tonnes in the medium and long term. Topco has orders worth about TWD 7.5 billion and plans to raise its production capacity in Taiwan by 30%, with production expected to start in the first quarter of 2027. Commercial Times separately reports its monthly capacity has risen from 80 to 140 tank trucks and will rise to 170 next year, figures it does not reconcile with the 30% increase; the demand it targets is for tank trucks and storage tanks linked to the expansion of Taiwanese wafer fabs and nearby specialty chemical plants. The reporting gives no detail for Sanfu Chemical beyond the expansion, no investment figures, and no revenue base for the 109% increase.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

These are materials and equipment suppliers expanding for electronic and semiconductor demand, including advanced packaging and the circuit-board materials beneath them. Advanced packaging and copper clad laminates use specialty resins, encapsulants and bonding materials, which is a general reading rather than something the report states. The Zhuhai line shows that a Taiwanese supplier is adding capacity in mainland China for this chain, which may indicate, on a general reading, that the supply base is following customers rather than staying in one place. A 109% monthly rise on an unstated base is a direction, not a size. Points that may be worth considering include how capacity for electronics materials in Taiwan and southern China is developing relative to demand, and whether expansion by local materials suppliers changes competition for specifications in advanced packaging.

Commercial Times

item.title: The OECD has raised its 2026 growth forecast for Germany to 1.1% from 0.7% in June, and kept its 2027 forecast at 1.1%.
item.description:
OECD economist Robert Grundke is quoted saying German exports rose surprisingly strongly in the first half of 2026, partly because of demand for electronic products and equipment linked to the AI boom, and that this demand is likely to remain high. Tagesschau adds that rising public investment in defence and infrastructure has also supported the recovery, and that the OECD refers to reforms of public procurement and faster planning and approval procedures for infrastructure projects. For comparison, the OECD expects the euro area to grow 1.0% this year and the world economy 2.9%, slightly above its June figures, while it has lowered its global 2027 outlook to 3.0% from 3.1% because the energy shock from the Middle East conflict is becoming more entrenched. The reporting does not break the German forecast down by sector or say what it assumes for energy prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The revision is driven by exports of electronics and by public spending on defence and infrastructure, which, on a general reading, are not the sectors that have carried German industrial demand in the past; the reporting does not mention automotive or private construction as drivers. A higher forecast built on those sources points to growth in some German customer segments; the reporting does not say whether others stay under pressure. Infrastructure and defence spending are also construction and equipment demand, where bonding and sealing are used, on a general reading. A forecast is not an outcome, and the OECD says the Middle East energy shock is weighing on the global outlook for 2027. Points that may be worth considering include how German demand plans weight electronics, infrastructure and defence against automotive, and whether faster approval procedures change the timing of infrastructure demand.

Handelsblatt | Tagesschau | Wallstreet:online | MarketScreener

item.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US and China have agreed to extend their trade truce, agreed at Busan, from 10 November to 10 January, keeping the suspension of additional tariffs on Chinese goods in place for a further two months.
item.description:
Bessent announced the extension after meeting Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, at the start of President Xi Jinping's state visit; CBC reports that Trump met Xi planeside at Joint Base Andrews. CBC also reports that under the truce the two countries agreed to scale back tariffs and refrain from new trade restrictions. The Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that if the agreement had expired, China would also have expanded its export controls on rare earths. Bessent indicated that further announcements could follow in the coming days, such as possible deals in financial services and agreements for China to buy more US agricultural products, and earlier said the US was open to a larger trade deal. The reporting does not say whether any tariff rates change, whether the rare-earth controls are formally postponed or simply not expanded, or what is expected to happen by 10 January.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The immediate effect is that the November cliff is removed: the tariff schedule between the two economies stays where it is for two more months, and the rare-earth escalation that would have come with expiry is not triggered, according to one report. A two-month horizon is short compared with the time needed for a sourcing change or a customer qualification, so for planning it moves the date rather than settles the question. The further announcements Bessent said could follow — possible financial-services deals and Chinese purchases of US farm products — are the part of the summit that could go beyond postponing a decision. Points that may be worth considering include which US–China product flows would have been affected by expiry on 10 November, whether 10 January falls inside current contract and budget periods, and what the summit produces beyond the extension.

Anadolu Agency | Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | Süddeutsche Zeitung | The Standard | CBC

item.title: Dataforce figures show Chinese brands took almost 12% of new-car sales in Europe in August 2026, a record share, while the overall market grew 4.6% as demand for hybrid and battery-electric cars rose 27%.
item.description:
Dataforce's region covers the EU, the EFTA countries and the UK. Chinese brands accounted for about one in four hybrid sales and one in three plug-in hybrid sales, which Lianhe Zaobao links to these models not being affected by the EU's high tariffs. Commercial Times reports Chinese brands at more than a fifth of new cars in the UK and 6.4% in Germany. Growth in hybrid and electric models offset declines in cars that run only on fuel. The manufacturers' association ACEA gives a separate EU-only series: registrations up 3% in July and 4.5% in August year on year, and up 5.3% to 7.55 million cars after eight months, with pure electric cars at 21.7% of the total, nearly six percentage points more than a year earlier, and plug-in hybrids at one tenth. The two series cover different regions and are not combined here. The reporting does not give Chinese brands' unit volumes or say which models drive the share, naming only BYD among the brands.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A growing market with a rising Chinese share means European registrations are growing while an increasing part of the vehicles come from Chinese brands — though the reporting does not say where the cars sold were built. For a supplier, that matters because assembly location determines which plants consume materials and whose approval lists a supplier needs to be on. The route through hybrids and plug-in hybrids, which avoid the EU tariffs, shows how trade rules shape the drivetrain mix Chinese brands bring to Europe, and drivetrain mix affects bonding, sealing and thermal-management content on a general reading. Points that may be worth considering include how much European automotive volume assumptions rely on European-built models, what qualification positions exist with the Chinese brands gaining share, and whether EU trade measures extend to hybrids.

Yahoo! Finance Canada | Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | Yahoo! Germany | Wallstreet:online

item.title: AWA Alexander Watson Associates' Corey Reardon names growth in Asia as a top trend for label and package printing over the next five years, calling it the fastest-growing region, driven by India, China and Southeast Asia.
item.description:
Reardon is AWA's president and chief executive, and the view was published by FINAT. Reardon names the growth of e-commerce and parcel delivery in Asia, such as Shopee in Southeast Asia and Blink-It in India, as a major driver for the growth of VIP labels used in shipping and distribution. Asian dominance is expected to continue over the forecast period 2026–2029. The reporting gives only this one trend of those AWA identifies, and no market size, growth rate or regional share, so the scale of the Asian lead is not visible. It is a market adviser's view, not a measurement, and it does not say how European or North American label demand is expected to develop over the same period.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Shipping and distribution labels are pressure-sensitive labels, so the trend described sits directly in a self-adhesive label market that uses adhesive technologies; that link is a general reading rather than something the report states. A shift of label growth towards Asian e-commerce points to growth in shipping and distribution labels applied at high speed in logistics, a segment where, on a general reading, cost and machine performance matter more than decoration. The absence of any figure means the trend gives a direction, not a size, and it comes from one adviser. Points that may be worth considering include how label-stock and adhesive supply in India and Southeast Asia is positioned against e-commerce logistics demand, and what AWA's full trend list says about the European market.

FINAT

item.title: European benchmark diesel futures rose up to 7% to USD 1,528 a tonne in London on 23 September after President Trump said he had told his administration "let's not send out the diesel", before falling back to USD 1,494 a tonne.
item.description:
The Financial Times reports that prices eased as Energy Secretary Chris Wright expressed doubts about the merits of a full ban. The same day, Politico reported, citing five people familiar with the discussions, that the administration was preparing a 90-day diesel export ban; a White House official called the report "fake news", and Wright said a blanket ban would not work and could push up gasoline and jet fuel prices, while the US was discussing voluntary measures. US ultra-low-sulphur diesel futures fell by more than 6% on the Politico report. Wallstreet:online reports that the prospect of a US export stop took Brent back above USD 100 a barrel. The background is a US diesel price of USD 6.51 a gallon on the American Automobile Association's figures, US refineries running at 97% of capacity, and domestic diesel stocks almost 13% below the five-year average for the time of year, according to Cnyes. For Europe, Transport & Environment puts the extra cost of road diesel to the EU economy at about EUR 40 billion since the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, and El Correo reports that diesel is about 43% of all petroleum product consumption in the EU. The reporting does not show that any ban has been decided, and beyond the 90-day duration in the Politico report gives no start date or destination scope.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The price reaction is the measurable part: a presidential remark moved European diesel by several percent within hours, and, according to the Financial Times, the Energy Secretary's scepticism about a full ban took part of it back the same day. That shows how exposed the European price is to US policy signals while European refining capacity is short, and El Correo's 43% share describes how much of EU petroleum product consumption sits in the product being moved. For a manufacturer, the exposure runs through road freight for inbound materials and outbound distribution, where, on a general reading, the cost arrives through carrier surcharges rather than directly. Nothing has been decided, and the two US signals point in different directions. Points that may be worth considering include how quickly fuel surcharges in European freight contracts follow a move in diesel futures, and whether logistics budgets assume the current level or allow for policy-driven swings of this size.

Financial Times | LiveMint | The Economic Times | Wallstreet:online | Cnyes | Anadolu Agency | El Correo

item.title: German specialty chemicals company Evonik has confirmed it will cut about 3,200 jobs by the end of 2029, 2,150 of them in Germany, as part of the largest restructuring in the company's history.
item.description:
The company says it aims to focus more on profitable business areas, and Tagesschau names aerospace, automotive supply, hydrogen and health technology. All six of Evonik's major German production sites are to be given specialised tasks, and the restructuring programme is to be fully implemented by 2030. The reporting does not say which business lines or sites carry the cuts, whether any production units will close or be sold, what the programme is expected to save, or how the cuts are phased between now and 2029. It also gives no statement from employee representatives. The reporting does not give Evonik's total headcount, so the share of the workforce affected cannot be worked out from these figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Evonik is a supplier of specialty chemicals, and on a general reading rather than anything in the report, some of its product families are raw materials for adhesive technologies formulators. A restructuring that assigns each German site a specialised task can change which site makes which product, and, on a general reading, site changes of that kind usually raise qualification and continuity questions for customers, even when the product specification does not change. The named focus areas — aerospace, automotive supply, hydrogen and health technology — describe where the company wants to grow; the reporting does not say which activities it wants to reduce, and that is the part that would matter to a buyer. The reporting gives a focus on more profitable business areas as the aim, not cost pressure; whether the cuts also reflect cost conditions for German chemical production is a general reading, not something the report states. Points that may be worth considering include which Evonik-supplied inputs are made at which German sites, whether any of them sit outside the named focus areas, and whether supply agreements anticipate a change of production site.

Tagesschau
